summary:
Helix Mission is a 4-player cooperative space mission and systems-engineering web game designed in a classic 16-bit retro aesthetic. Players take on asymmetric astronaut roles—Engineer, Navigator, Life-Support Officer, and Mission Commander—to plan, launch, and survive an emergency Mars-support mission across five story-driven chapters.

The game directly addresses the Space Mission Design challenge by transforming abstract aerospace constraints into tactile, cooperative gameplay. Starting on Earth, players select spacecraft components, balance mass, power, budget, and fuel, and physically transport propellant modules while respecting launch limits. During launch and deep-space transit, crews monitor live telemetry, solve physics-linked navigation equations, manage closed-loop waste and water recycling, and perform urgent system repairs triggered by realistic spaceflight hazards rather than random sabotage. Upon reaching Mars, teams must allocate scarce power to build radiation shields and sustain life support during a solar storm.

Helix Mission makes real human-spaceflight engineering accessible and engaging. Instead of simple win-or-lose outcomes, a detailed post-mission debrief explains how every design trade-off affected survival—teaching players why resource efficiency, closed-loop sustainability, and teamwork are essential for future Moon-to-Mars exploration.

Project Details: Helix Mission

1. What does it do and how does it work?

Helix Mission is an interactive 4-player cooperative (and solo-capable) space mission design and survival simulation game rendered in a 16-bit retro aesthetic. Players step into the boots of an emergency Mars-support crew divided into four asymmetric roles: Mission Commander, Engineer, Navigator, and Life-Support Officer.

The experience unfolds across five interconnected mission chapters:

  • Chapter 1 — Earth Preparation & Assembly: Teams define mission parameters, budget their resources, select spacecraft components, locate the proper propellant module in storage, and physically transport it to the launchpad without exceeding launch-mass limits.
  • Chapter 2 — Launch Countdown & Telemetry: As the rocket prepares for liftoff, each role monitors real-time telemetry (fuel pressure, battery levels, engine temperature, structural stress, and navigation alignment) to resolve pre-launch anomalies under time pressure.
  • Chapter 3 — Deep-Space Transit & Hazard Repairs: En route to Mars, realistic spaceflight hazards—vibration, radiation spikes, thermal stress, and earlier design trade-offs—trigger urgent repair tasks (rewiring power buses, replacing blown fuses, realigning solar arrays, and patching air leaks).
  • Chapter 4 — Closed-Loop Waste & Resource Management: Crews actively manage onboard consumables by compacting waste, recycling water, reusing materials for repairs, or converting organic matter into fertilizer—directly impacting spacecraft mass, storage capacity, and crew health.
  • Chapter 5 — Mars Habitat Survival & Solar Storm Defense: Upon arrival at Mars, players discover elevated radiation and depleted life-support capacity. They must ration scarce power to construct radiation shielding, maintain water/air recycling, sustain food production, and keep communications with Earth active until resupply arrives.

2. What benefits does it have?

  • Turns Abstract Physics into Tangible Gameplay: Rather than treating mass, power, and budget as static numbers on a spreadsheet, every engineering choice has physical consequences—such as heavier fuel tanks slowing down ground transport and requiring more complex trajectory calculations during flight.
  • Builds Authentic Teamwork & Communication: Because each of the four roles controls critical, interdependent systems, no single player can succeed alone. Teams must negotiate trade-offs, prioritize emergencies, and coordinate resource allocation in real time.
  • Accessible STEM Education: Complex aerospace concepts—including Tsiolkovsky mass ratios, closed-loop Environmental Control and Life Support Systems (ECLSS), and space radiation shielding—are introduced intuitively through hands-on mini-games and clear visual telemetry.

3. What is the intended impact of the project?

Helix Mission is designed to inspire students, educators, and space enthusiasts to think like real NASA systems engineers. By framing human spaceflight around realistic Moon-to-Mars hazards (radiation, isolation, closed-loop sustainability, and resource scarcity), the game shifts the player's mindset from simple arcade action to sustainable deep-space exploration. Our post-mission multi-ending evaluation report teaches players why a mission succeeded or fell short, reinforcing systems thinking, resource stewardship, and collaborative problem-solving.

4. What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

vibe coding

  • Hardware & Collaboration: Developed on standard consumer laptops using Git/GitHub for version control and browser-based testing across desktop environments.

5. How is your project creative?

  • Hazard-Driven Tasks Instead of Random Sabotage: While inspired by cooperative social-deduction games, Helix Mission replaces arbitrary sabotage with realistic aerospace failure modes caused by player design choices and deep-space hazards.
  • Closed-Loop Waste as a Core Mechanic: Few space games model waste management; Helix Mission treats every kilogram of unrecycled waste as a direct threat to storage capacity, spacecraft mass, and scientific payload capability.
  • Multi-Ending Diagnostic Debrief: Instead of a binary "Win/Lose" screen, the game generates tailored outcomes (Perfect Mission, Scientific Success, Emergency Survival, or Mission Failure) with specific engineering feedback explaining how earlier trade-offs shaped the final result.

6. What factors did your team consider?

  • NASA Challenge Alignment: We carefully mapped our game mechanics to NASA’s core human spaceflight challenges—specifically closed-loop life support, radiation protection, launch mass constraints, and power budgeting.
  • Replayability & Non-Linear Solutions: We ensured there is no single "correct" rocket build; players can succeed through different combinations of lightweight/expensive or heavy/budget components if they adapt their in-flight strategy.
  • Accessibility & Pacing: We designed the game to support both 4-player team lobbies and a seamless solo mode, pairing simple retro visuals with progressive chapter difficulty so players of any technical background can jump in immediately.
